reckons.claim: There's stacks of robot hype and doom in the extremes. We think it'll land somewhere in the middle. Because it usually does.
This is a lot of years in a little chapter so we've pulled the bits that click together best. History was messier than this.
Nobody actually knows why nerds love chess. But there's some reasonable stuff we can assume.
We've kept the big numbers deliberately loose. Nobody hand counted all the books in all the libraries.
We know who was there and what happened next. We're guessing at what they were thinking at the time.
This tech changes all the time. Top line, the robots are more similar than different. But they'll all tell you they're special in their own way.
Whether or not the robots think is more philosophy than science. Our take is that memory and math doesn't make them Plato.
Token economics is a moving target. This is more about how tokens work than where the money will land.
'Better chats beat better prompts' is an opinion based on experience. You'll easily find people who believe just the opposite.
We reckon training is the big unlock. Because it usually is.
The basics of how to customise robots are sound. The language will likely bounce around, bot by bot over time.
Nobody knows what tomorrow will throw. But we do know what's less likely. So we've stacked the doom in order from catastrophe to creeper.
Workslop is a term coined by management consultants and is now widely uttered as an under-breath expletive.
Our big assumption is that history repeats. We don't know that it will. It just always has before.
Agents are usually smarter than puppies. The watch out is supervision, not intelligence.
It's true that robots do what they do by stealing. So the question we're really asking is who's committing the crime.
Nobody knows why the em-dash became a thing. But people like to know why odd stuff happens. So we've given it a go with guesswork.
We cherry picked three stories to make a point. History is never that tidy. Plus robots having original ideas is about how you define 'original'.
Ethics needs another twenty books. We haven't done it justice. The basic idea is write the rules before you play the game.
Again we've based the fortune telling on the clues we get from history. Past returns aren't proof of future performance.
The idea that people don't change is evolutionary jazz hands. Individuals change all the time. As a species, we just left the cave.
All the previous assumptions wrapped into a promise that's really a guess. But the big point is that the robots are here. Let's play.
